newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lankan opposition says go slow on constitution.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lankan opposition says go slow on constitution.

text.p: Sri Lanka's main opposition party on Saturday accused the government of forging ahead with constitutional reform without the full consent of a parliamentary select committee studying the package.

"Members of the select committee have only agreed on some issues so far. There are issues which they have disagreed on and issues which still have not been discussed," said Gamini Atukorala, general secretary of the United National Party (UNP).
"While select committee proceedings are still going on, the government has decided to publish some parts of the draft constitution. We disagree with that," Atukorala told Reuters.

The UNP's support is crucial for the government, which has a majority of just one in Sri Lanka's 225-seat parliament, if it is to get the two-thirds majority required in the house to pass the proposals.

The government of President Chandrika Kumaratunga this week released sections of a draft constitution which in its full form would offer wide autonomy to Sri Lanka's minorities and aims to end the country's 13-year ethnic war.
Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam rebels are waging a violent campaign for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the north and east of the island.

Justice and Constitutional Affairs Minister Gamini Lakshman Peiris said 18 chapters of the draft constitution were being released, but a key chapter on devolution of power was held back as this was still being debated by the select committee.

The proposals regarding the devolution of power were expected to be completed within the next few weeks and the new constitutional package as a whole would be placed before parliament within the next couple of months, Peiris said.
But Atukorala said the UNP had not yet consented to some of the issues, as the party was looking at the proposed changes to the constitution as a whole.
"You can't make public something which in totality has not been agreed upon by all members (of the select committee). You can't put out bits and pieces of a new constitution," he said.
He did not identify the issues the UNP disagreed with, but said the party planned to take up the matter when the select committee meets again on April 8.
If approved by parliament, the new constitution will be put to the people in a national referendum.
